Preamble

Now that Wine is installed, you'll need to create a Wineprefix to store and run your Windows applications. You can created multiple Wineprefixes, one for each Windows application you intend to install, or just throw everything into a single prefix and hope for the best. The choice is fully yours.

As for where on disk you can create a Wineprefix, the answer is pretty much anywhere. You can even create the prefix on an external hard drive, so long as your operating system has mounted and can read/write to the drive using your default user account.

The default location Wine is set to use for its Wineprefix is: /home/{Your_Username}/.wine

If the .wine folder does not exist (.folders are hidden by default) then Wineboot will be used to create and populate the directory, providing you haven't specified somewhere else to setup the Wineprefix.

Creating a new Wineprefix

In this guide, I'll demonstrate how to create two new Wineprefixes within the User's home directory, one for 32-bit, the other 64-bit.

Note: While wineboot is creating the prefix, you'll probably see a lot of err and fixme messages being outputted to the terminal. Unless the process stops, these can be ignored.

32-bit Wineprefix

To start with, launch a terminal session and enter the following:

WINEARCH=win32 WINEPREFIX=~/win32 winecfg

WINEARCH has been declared and set to win32, so that wineboot knows to create the new Wineprefix as a 32-bit Windows prefix. ~/win32 tells wineboot that the Wineprefix is to be placed in your homefolder in a new folder named win32. If it does not exist, Wine will automatically create it.

If successful, you should notice the win32 folder has been created and populated with the required directory structure and Windows system files created by the Wine project.

As we specified winecfg at the end of the command, instead of just "wineboot", the Wine Configuration window should have automatically launched, after wineboot had finished setting up the prefix, which will grant you the ability to modify the new Wineprefixes' settings (discussed further along in this guide).

64-bit Wineprefix

To start with, launch a terminal session and enter the following:

WINEARCH=win64 WINEPREFIX=~/win64 winecfg

WINEARCH has been declared and set to win64, this is not strictly needed, as Wine will create win64 Wineprefixes by default, but if you're like me, and try to be as specific as possible when issuing commands, you can keep that part in. ~/win64 tells wineboot that the Wineprefix is to be placed in your homefolder in a new folder named win64. If it does not exist, Wine will automatically create it.

If successful, you should notice the win64 folder has been created and populated with the required directory structure and Windows system files created by the Wine project. As on a true Windows 64-bit system, you should notice Program Files and Program Files (X86) folders are present. The Windows Registry created for this prefix will likewise contain the WOW6432Node.

As we specified winecfg in the command, instead of just "wineboot", the Wine Configuration window should have automatically launched, after wineboot had finished setting up the preix, which will grant you the ability to modify the new Wineprefixes' settings (discussed further along in this guide).

Winecfg Interface Overview

At last, we get to use a GUI, is what I guess some of you are thinking, but all I'm thinking is, fuck, this is going to be annoying to explain without pictures, so here we go.

The Interface (Tabs)

Drives

Here you can change which drives are mapped and to where for the Wineprefix. A Windows executable launched within the prefix will use the information set here to determine where the C, D and other drives are located.

By default, C: is mapped to the drive_c folder within the Wineprefix. D: is set for your CD/DVD Drive, at /dev/sr0, if you have one present. (Click on Show Advanced to see these settings).

Crucially, Z: is mapped to your root directory /, meaning any application running in your Wineprefix can see the rest of Linux installation and any additional drives you have mapped/attached.

This is one of the reasons why it is important to never run wine as the root user.

Audio

Here you can change the various input and output devices. Depending on your setup, Wine will typically be using the winepulse.drv driver, meaning sound within your Wineprefix is using PulseAudio.

In many cases, this is not an issue, but some games will suffer from choppy or stuttering sound when using PulseAudio. To resolve this, you can switch to using Alsa, if you have the required software packages installed. See the example at the end of this guide.

Staging (if using Wine Staging)

Here you can tick various check boxes to enable or disable certain staging features, or other patches, if your Wine installation included additional patches.

A Wine-Staging package, including the Gallium 9 patches, for example, would have a check box marked: Enable Gallium Nine for better D3D9 graphic performance, in addition to the standard Staging Settings options.

About (the most exciting tab)

Yay, it's glass of Wine! Plus you can also specify the Owner and Organisation values that Windows applications will see, when run within the Wineprefix. Not really needed, in my experience.

Applications

Here you can create Application-Specific Settings Profiles. By clicking Add application, you can locate a Windows executable already installed in the Wineprefix and set some settings to be explicitly applied, when that application is run.

The libraries and graphics tabs are linked, so for example, you could have a Windows Application inside the Wineprefix set to Windows XP, when it runs, set to a specific, low resolution, and to override specific DLLs, when compared to the other applications running within the Wineprefix.

Libraries

The most important and annoying tab. Here you can specify Prefix-Wide and Application-Specific overrides for certain DLLs. By default, Wine will always attempt to load the Built-in (Wine version) of a DLL, but some Wine DLLs are not feature complete, or turn out buggy for certain applications. Here you can specify which DLLs you want to override (set to Native). This will be explained in greater details in the Overrides Guide.

Graphics

The Graphics tab allows you to set mouse capture behaviour, whether or not Wine should emulate a virtual desktop (useful for older applications that don't scale well to full screen), as well as changing the DPI settings.

Desktop Integration

Lastly, the Desktop Integration tab allows you to change the theme being applied to Wine. (Themes installed separately.)

You can also change where the Desktop, My Documents etc... folders are linked to.

Wine Control

Wine Control aims to replicate some of the functionality of the Windows Control Panel.

You run it by entering the following into the terminal:

wine control

Or, if targetting a specific Wineprefix, other than the default one:

WINEPREFIX=/path/to/your/prefix wine control

Here you can Add/Remove programs, and see what joysticks/controllers have been detected by Wine and test if they are working correctly.

You can also access the Windows' Internet Settings, should an application need specific settings applied there.

Wine Regedit

This is a pretty straightforward one for Ex-Windows Users. This application replicates the functionality of the Windows' Regedit utility and can be used to add/modify/delete information stored within the Wineprefixes' registry.

Examples of Common Tasks

Changing the Audio Driver used from Pulseaudio to Alsa

As previously mentioned, Pulsaudio can cause issues in some cases, and rather than messing around with Pulseaudio, it is sometimes quicker to just default to Alsa.

To get Alsa as an option, you must first ensure you have the following packages installed:

Arch Linux (Arch Based Distributions) - lib32-alsa-lib and lib32-alsa-plugins

Ubuntu Linux (Ubuntu Based Distributions) - alsa-base

Solus Linux - alsa-lib-32bit and alsa-plugins-32bit

Ensure you have run winecfg at least once within your Wineprefix, to create the required entries in the registry (or you can manually create them). Close winecfg if you have it open.

From the terminal run:

WINEPREFIX=/path/to/your/prefix regedit

When the registry opens, navigate to:

HKCU\Software\Wine\Drivers

Create a new entry (String) called Audio and set the value to "alsa" without the quotes.

Close regedit and run winecfg in your Wineprefix again. You should now see, in the Audio tab, the winealsa.drv being used, along with all the input and output devices it detected.

Changing the Default Wineprefix Location

As mentioned previously, Wine's default Wineprefix location is /home/{Your_Username}/.wine, but what if you do not want to use that folder. How do you change that?

The answer is, you can't, not directly. To get around this is you'd move the .wine directory to the location you want to use instead, and then create a symbolic link to the new location.

For example:

ln -s /media/games/.wine ~/.wine

Will create a link in /home/{Your_Username}/.wine that will redirect to /media/games/.wine.

Just make sure you have ownership of the directory structure in the new location, otherwise Wine will complain you do not have the required permissions to write changes.
